items.prompt_md: In the iterative k-group reversal, what is `group_prev`?
options: The first node of the current block
The node just before the current block, which is the tail of the already-finished part
The last node of the whole list
A copy of the head used only for returning
items.answer: The node just before the current block, which is the tail of the already-finished part
items.explanation_md: `group_prev` is where the reversed block is re-attached on the left. The block's first node changes during reversal, and the head is a different pointer.

items.prompt_md: Why do we walk `k` nodes ahead before reversing a block?
options: To confirm the block is complete, because fewer than `k` remaining nodes must be left untouched
To find the middle of the list
To count the total length of the list
Because reversal needs the nodes in an array
items.answer: To confirm the block is complete, because fewer than `k` remaining nodes must be left untouched
items.explanation_md: Reversing first and undoing after a failed check is error-prone and costs extra pointer work. A quick forward walk avoids both.

items.prompt_md: Why use a dummy node in front of the head?
options: It stores the length of the list
It makes the reversal run in O(log n)
It avoids recursion
The first block then has a `group_prev` like every other, so no special case is needed and `dummy.next` is the new head
items.answer: The first block then has a `group_prev` like every other, so no special case is needed and `dummy.next` is the new head
items.explanation_md: After the first block is reversed, the original head is no longer the head, and the dummy keeps a stable handle on the front. The dummy has nothing to do with complexity.

items.prompt_md: Inside the block reversal, `prev` starts as `group_next` (the node after the block) rather than `None`. What does this achieve?
options: It skips the first node of the block
It makes the block circular
When the loop ends, the block's old first node already points at the rest of the list, so only the block's new front needs wiring
It reverses the rest of the list as well
items.answer: When the loop ends, the block's old first node already points at the rest of the list, so only the block's new front needs wiring
items.explanation_md: The first node processed gets `next = prev = group_next`, which is exactly the link the tail needs. Starting from `None` would force an extra reconnect step.

items.prompt_md: After reversing the block `A → B → C` (k = 3) so it reads `C → B → A`, which node becomes the next `group_prev`?
options: `C`, the new front
`A`, the old first node that is now the tail of the reversed block
`B`, the middle node
The dummy node
items.answer: `A`, the old first node that is now the tail of the reversed block
items.explanation_md: The next block begins right after `A`, so `A` is the node whose `next` must be redirected when that block is reversed.

items.prompt_md: What does the algorithm do with a final group of fewer than `k` nodes?
options: Leaves it exactly as it is and returns `dummy.next`
Reverses it anyway
Deletes it
Moves it to the front
items.answer: Leaves it exactly as it is and returns `dummy.next`
items.explanation_md: The check fails inside the walk-ahead loop, and the function returns immediately. Reversing a short tail would be a different problem (some variants require it, with a one-line change).

items.prompt_md: What is the time complexity of reversing a list of `n` nodes in k-groups iteratively?
options: O(n * k), since each block costs k and there are n blocks
O(n^2 / k), because of re-walking from the head
O(k)
O(n): each node is touched a constant number of times, about once by the length check and once by the reversal
items.answer: O(n): each node is touched a constant number of times, about once by the length check and once by the reversal
items.explanation_md: There are about `n / k` blocks and each costs O(k) work, so the product is O(n), not O(n*k). Re-walking from the head to find predecessors would give the quadratic bound, but `group_prev` avoids that.

items.prompt_md: What extra space does the iterative solution use?
options: O(k) for a buffer of the block
O(n) for an array of node values
O(1): a handful of pointers (`dummy`, `group_prev`, `kth`, `group_next`, `prev`, `cur`)
O(n / k) for a stack of blocks
items.answer: O(1): a handful of pointers (`dummy`, `group_prev`, `kth`, `group_next`, `prev`, `cur`)
items.explanation_md: Nodes are relinked in place, so no buffer is needed. The O(n/k) figure belongs to the recursive version.

items.prompt_md: A recursive version reverses the first `k` nodes and recurses on the remainder. What extra space does it use?
options: O(1), since the recursion is a tail call in Python
O(n / k) stack frames, one per block
O(k) only
items.answer: O(n / k) stack frames, one per block
items.explanation_md: Each call handles one block and leaves its frame on the stack until the recursion unwinds. Python does not eliminate tail calls, and the depth is the block count.

items.prompt_md: What does the function return for `k = 1`?
options: The list unchanged, since each block of one node reverses to itself
An empty list
The reversed list
Only the first node
items.answer: The list unchanged, since each block of one node reverses to itself
items.explanation_md: A block of size 1 reversed is itself, so every relink is a no-op in effect. It is a good edge case to mention in an interview.

items.prompt_md: For a list of 7 nodes and `k = 3`, which nodes end up in a different position than they started?
options: All seven nodes
Only the first three nodes
Only the middle node of each block
The first six nodes (two reversed blocks); the seventh stays as the tail
items.answer: The first six nodes (two reversed blocks); the seventh stays as the tail
items.explanation_md: Two full blocks fit and are reversed, while the lone leftover is skipped. The middle node of each block is the one that stays in place within the block.

items.prompt_md: If you forget `group_prev.next = kth` after reversing a block, what happens?
options: Nothing, because reversal reconnects it automatically
The loop never terminates for k = 1
`group_prev` still points at the old first node (now the block's tail), so the rest of the reversed block becomes unreachable from the head
The list becomes circular
items.answer: `group_prev` still points at the old first node (now the block's tail), so the rest of the reversed block becomes unreachable from the head
items.explanation_md: Reversal fixes the links among block nodes and to what follows, but nothing re-points the left neighbour to the new front. The block is silently cut out.

items.prompt_md: Reverse every consecutive group of 4 nodes in a singly linked list, in place, leaving a trailing group shorter than 4 as is.
options: Copy values into an array and rewrite the nodes
Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
Fast and slow pointers to find the middle
Merge with a dummy head
items.answer: Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
items.explanation_md: Block-wise in-place reversal with reconnection is the k-group technique. Copying values uses O(n) space and is often forbidden; fast/slow and merging solve different list problems.

items.prompt_md: Swap every two adjacent nodes of a list by changing links, not values.
options: The k-group technique with k = 2 (a dummy head, and reconnecting after each pair)
Fast and slow pointers
A hash set of seen nodes
Reverse the whole list once
items.answer: The k-group technique with k = 2 (a dummy head, and reconnecting after each pair)
items.explanation_md: Swapping pairs is reversal of blocks of size 2 with the same group_prev bookkeeping. A single full reversal would reverse the entire order rather than each pair.

items.prompt_md: Process a list in blocks whose sizes grow 1, 2, 3, ... and reverse only the blocks of even length (the last block may be short).
options: Sorting the nodes by value
A monotonic stack of node values
Binary search on the list
Group-wise in-place reversal: compute each block's real length first, reverse it if even, reconnect via `group_prev`
items.answer: Group-wise in-place reversal: compute each block's real length first, reverse it if even, reconnect via `group_prev`
items.explanation_md: The block size changes but the mechanics (bounded reversal and reconnecting both ends) are the k-group ones. Sorting or stack tricks do not preserve the required structure.

items.prompt_md: Rearrange a list so that each consecutive run of 5 nodes appears backwards, using O(1) extra memory, and do not touch a final run of 3.
options: Recursion that stores each run in a list
Build a new list from a reversed array copy
Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
Two pointers moving inward on the array
items.answer: Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
items.explanation_md: In-place constant memory and an untouched short tail both point at the iterative k-group routine. Building arrays or new lists breaks the O(1) constraint.

items.prompt_md: Re-link a list so each pair of neighbouring nodes is flipped, and the problem statement says node values must not be modified.
options: Swap the `val` fields of each pair
Relink nodes in pairs with a dummy head (k-group, k = 2)
Binary search for the pair
Convert to a heap
items.answer: Relink nodes in pairs with a dummy head (k-group, k = 2)
items.explanation_md: Because values are off limits, you relink. Swapping `val` would be simpler but violates the rule.

items.prompt_md: Reverse an entire singly linked list in place.
options: Plain in-place reversal with `prev`, `cur`, `next` (no blocks)
Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
Recursion with a hash map
Sorting the nodes
items.answer: Plain in-place reversal with `prev`, `cur`, `next` (no blocks)
items.explanation_md: A single pass with three pointers is enough. The block bookkeeping (group_prev, kth) only pays off when you reverse several segments.

items.prompt_md: Return the middle node of a linked list in a single pass without counting its length first.
options: Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
Reverse the list, then walk
A monotonic stack
Fast and slow pointers
items.answer: Fast and slow pointers
items.explanation_md: When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow one is at the middle. No reversal is involved.

items.prompt_md: In an array, reverse every consecutive chunk of 3 elements, leaving a trailing partial chunk alone.
options: Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
A min-heap
Swap-from-both-ends two pointers inside each chunk
Fast and slow pointers
items.answer: Swap-from-both-ends two pointers inside each chunk
items.explanation_md: Arrays have random access, so reversing a chunk is two indices swapping toward each other. The linked-list relinking machinery is unnecessary.

items.prompt_md: Reverse the order of the words in a sentence stored in a mutable character array, in place.
options: Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
Two pointers: reverse the whole array, then reverse each word
Merge with a dummy head
A trie
items.answer: Two pointers: reverse the whole array, then reverse each word
items.explanation_md: It is array reversal at two granularities, solved with swapping pointers; there are no nodes or next pointers to reconnect.

items.prompt_md: Given a string of brackets, decide whether every opening bracket is closed in the right order.
options: A stack of open brackets
Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
Fast and slow pointers
Prefix sums
items.answer: A stack of open brackets
items.explanation_md: Last-opened, first-closed is stack behaviour. Nothing here is a linked list that needs relinking.

items.prompt_md: Combine two sorted linked lists into one sorted list by relinking nodes.
options: Per block: dummy head, check k nodes exist, reverse in place, reconnect both ends
Reverse the second list first
A max-heap
Merge with a dummy head
items.answer: Merge with a dummy head
items.explanation_md: Two sorted inputs are merged by repeatedly appending the smaller front node to a tail pointer behind a dummy. No reversal of blocks is involved.
